Informal guide to sculpting

To start I will say this, experiment, try new things, who knows what will give the best results until you figure it out. I have often suprised myself.

All Sculpey is not equal!

Original Sculpey -- white very soft, but also very easy to mold not much strength to hold itself up or in form Super Sculpey -- firmer with a bit more strength still fairly easy to work with, Good for smaller creations Super Sculpey Firm -- very firm(though if it has been sitting for a while in the store or your house you have to really work it in you hands before you can use it) good for fine details, this one can get 'brittle' and crack forcing you to work it back together

There really isn't a difference once you cook them so find which one you like most.

So to start I create the base and wireframe structure that will support the clay, allow me to adjust the pose if I don't like it and provide stability to the creation once its done. Typically i use galvanized 16 gauge steel wire(electric fence wire I had from when I made chainmail) and 20 gauge aluminum wire(homedepot and lowes look it the drop ceiling section)

Wire Frame

With the wireframe is done I'll wrap the thinker areas with aluminum foil, this helps reduce the amount of clay needed the sculpt making it easier to cook and cheaper.

Now that I have the frame to work from I will rough out a shape, mostly just covering the foil and wire and getting a rough idea of what I want the sculpture to look like. At this point I mostly work on shape, make sure the pose is one I like(the wire 'skeleton' actually allows a pretty wide flexibility in movement)

Base

I will used the base to build from adding different details as I go. From experience I learned to add inside details first.(like the under arm/side of torso before finishing the outside of the arm) This will keep you from messing out details as you try to reach the hard to get at places with you fingers and tools. Start with big details and work to finer and finer details, try textures or different looks, nothing is set in stone:) I like to think of it as I have a naked creature and I'm 'clothing' it with skin, horns, fur, armor.

Adding details

Poking with a needle in a stippling fashion will give a nice 'rough' look, doing the same with a dull tool will give you the hammered look I used in the behold armor plates.

Rough look

I used the knurling(the diamond pattern on metal tools the give it a grip) on the handle of one of my tools to make a quick easy chainmail pattern.

Chainmail

For fur I build the shape of the hair, then take a sharp tool and 'draw on' the hair in cuts. It will also blend the clay added to the base and if you cut up the edges give a nice rough look like clumps of hair. When working with small details; teeth, nails, horns, accessories, i find its easier to back these first and then add to you sculpture. It will keep these looking the same as you are working with other things and allows you to make the horns without worrying about putting wire in them or sagging when you cook it.

Fur and teeth

Wrinkles are a lot like fur, but I take a paintbrush and smooth over the lines and the add more until I get the look I am after. (Buy cheapo paintbrushes for this as the clay gums them up and you ruin the bristles)

Wrinkles

Adding thin strands to a surface and smoothing it down is the easiest way to make veins or folds

Veins

I will roll out thin flat sheets for clothing draping it over my figure, this allows you to add a texture or details to the piece before you put it on your creation. It also means if you don't like it you can pull it off and try again. Be sure when you are adding things the work anything together really well and avoid leaving sealed air gaps in your creature(trapped air can expand and cause bubbles/cracks when you cook it) If you have a trapped pocket of air poke a hole in a spot that can be smoothed or isn't seen to keep it from bubbling.

Clothing/accessories

Cooking

Sculpey should be cooked in an oven at 275F/130C for 15 minutes per 1/4 inch/6mm thickness of your clay. I will go off the thickest part as cooking a little longer doesn't affect it as much as under cooking it will. The thickness is from the foil core to the 'skin' of the creation not how thick the whole thing is. Be warns you will smell the sculpey as it is cooking so open windows. I use wood bases and if I have to glue anything elmer's glue, neither are phased by the oven. If you are using beads for eyes make sure they are glass. The sculpey will actually get softest as you are cooking it so keep an eye on things to make sure they don't droop or sag. Once it is done cooking let it sit for an hour or so to cool, while its hot it will still be a bit pliable but not much.

After its cool, check for cracks, if there are some a little glue into the crack will seal it right up.

Sanding is recommended to rid it of any fingerprints, tool marks, or flakes you don't want.

Painting

Start with a nice base coat of paint, to seal it and give you and even color to start. I'll typically use a black or brown as a base.

Base coat and painting

I find the using washes(thinning the paint with water) and the layering those on gives me a more realistic look. If I want to cover something I won't thin it as much or if I just want to add a bit I will thin it quite a bit. The thinner the wash the more it will collect in all the nooks and crannies. Start broad and fill in small details should be the last things painted.

Washes

Just my experience with this, there are tons of videos out there on how to do any of this and hundreds of really talented people doing it. I hope this helps give you a brief look into what goes into makes these kinds of sculptures. If you have any questions feel free to ask!
